The working directory persists between commands, but shell state does not. The shell environment is initialized from the user's profile (bash or zsh).

Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user:

 - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
 - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
 - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
 - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)

 - If your command will create new directories or files, first use this tool to run `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
 - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes in your command (e.g., cd "path with spaces/file.txt")
 - Try to maintain your current working directory throughout the session by using absolute paths and avoiding usage of `cd`. You may use `cd` if the User explicitly requests it. In particular, never prepend `cd <current-directory>` to a `git` command — `git` already operates on the current working tree, and the compound triggers a permission prompt.
 - You may specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). By default, your command will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
 - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. You do not need to use '&' at the end of the command when using this parameter.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

1	---
2	title: Notifications and digests requirements
3	id: REQ-NOTIFICATIONS
4	status: approved
5	owners: [product-team, t.abara]
6	last_updated: 2026-05-19
7	related: [REQ-095, REQ-111, ADR-005, DES-120]
8	---
9	
10	## Scope
11	
12	This document defines the requirements for in-app notifications, per-user preferences, and
13	the daily digest email: how domain events become notifications, who gets notified and who is
14	suppressed, read/unread state, and how the digest batches, windows and renders unread items
15	into one email. It does not define email rendering or delivery mechanics beyond what the
16	digest needs (`REQ-124`), nor webhook delivery, which has its own retry and backoff story in
17	`webhooks.md`.
18	
19	## Context
20	
21	`src/server/services/notification-service.ts` is the fan-out hub: a single call to
22	`notify(orgId, kind, recipients, payload)` produces zero or more in-app `Notification` rows,
23	filtered through each recipient's `NotificationPreference` (`notification-preference-repository.ts`)
24	and each recipient's applicable feature flags (`resolveChannels` takes a `FlagContext`
25	because the `digest_email` channel itself is plan-gated, per `REQ-120`). Notification
26	creation is not the same code path as the domain event that triggers it — `issue-service.ts`,
27	`comment-service.ts` and the rest never call `notify()` directly; they only `emit()` domain
28	events, and a set of listeners registered by `registerEventHandlers()` in
29	`event-registry.ts` are what translate those events into notification calls. This
30	indirection is what keeps `REQ-114` ("actors are not notified about their own actions")
31	enforceable in one place rather than duplicated at every emit site.
32	
33	`Notification` rows are per recipient and per organization (`REQ-110`); there is no
34	cross-org inbox, which follows the same tenancy discipline as everything else, and a user in
35	three organizations sees three separate notification counts, one per org, computed by
36	`countUnread(orgId, recipientId)`.
37	
38	The daily digest is a distinct concern layered on top: `digest-service.ts#buildDigest`
39	gathers every unread notification for a recipient inside a bounded window
40	(`digestWindow()` from `src/lib/date.ts`) and hands the bundle to `renderDigest`, which
41	produces an email via `renderEmail(template, props)` in `email-service.ts`. The digest job
42	(`digest-email-job.ts`) runs on the `digest-email` cadence (every 1440 minutes — once a day,
43	`CADENCE_MINUTES`), calling `shouldRunForOrg(org, now)` to decide whether this tick is the
44	org's digest hour before doing any real work — most ticks for most orgs are a no-op check,
45	not a digest send. `sendEmail` never performs network egress in this codebase; it writes the
46	rendered draft to the log, which is why the corpus can describe email delivery as a real
47	requirement (`REQ-124`) without needing an SMTP integration to back it.
48	
49	## Open questions
50	
51	1. `REQ-012` in `organizations.md` notes that `digestWindow` currently takes a
52	   `digestHourUtc` integer rather than a full timezone; every requirement in this document
53	   that references "the org's digest window" inherits that same UTC-hour-not-timezone
54	   limitation.
55	2. `REQ-115`'s preferences are per channel and per event class, but there is no requirement
56	   describing what happens when a recipient's only enabled channel for an event class is
57	   `digest_email` and the org's plan does not include `digest_email` (`REQ-120`) — whether
58	   that notification silently has no channel or falls back to in-app is not specified in
59	   code comments or tests.
60	3. Whether digest windows should be recomputed if an org changes its digest hour mid-cycle,
61	   potentially producing a very short or very long first window, is unresolved.
62	
63	### REQ-110 — Notifications are per recipient and per organization
64	
65	- **Priority:** must
66	- **Status:** implemented
67	- **Related:** REQ-010, REQ-118, DES-120
68	- **Implemented by:** `src/server/repositories/notification-repository.ts` — `listNotifications`, `countUnread`
69	- **Verified by:** `tests/services/notification-service.test.ts`
70	
71	`notifications` carries `org_id` and a `recipient_id`; every read (`listNotifications`,
72	`countUnread`) is scoped to both. A user who belongs to several organizations sees
73	independent notification state per org — reading everything unread in one org has no effect
74	on unread counts in another.
75	
76	**Acceptance criteria**
77	
78	1. `countUnread(orgId, recipientId)` never includes notifications from a different `orgId`
79	   even for the same recipient.
80	2. `listNotifications` requires both an actor (for authorization) and an implicit org scope
81	   derived from that actor.
82	3. Switching active organization (`REQ-009`) changes which notification set the inbox UI
83	   displays without any server-side notification data changing.
84	
85	### REQ-111 — Notification fan-out is driven by domain events
86	
87	- **Priority:** must
88	- **Status:** implemented
89	- **Related:** ADR-005, REQ-065, REQ-095
90	
91	Every notification in the product originates from a subscriber on the event bus
92	(`src/lib/event-bus.ts`), registered once via `registerEventHandlers()` and never called
93	inline from the service that emitted the triggering event. This indirection (`ADR-005`) is
94	what lets notification logic evolve — new recipient rules, new event types — without
95	touching `issue-service.ts`, `comment-service.ts` or any other emitter.
96	
97	**Acceptance criteria**
98	
99	1. No service outside the event-bus subscriber set calls `notify()` directly.
100	2. Registering a new listener for an existing event type does not require changing the
101	   emitter.
102	3. A subscriber's failure is isolated per the event bus's error-isolation guarantee and does
103	   not roll back the domain write that triggered the event.
104	
105	**Implemented by:** `src/server/services/notification-service.ts`, `src/server/services/event-registry.ts`
106	**Verified by:** `tests/services/notification-service.test.ts`
107	
108	### REQ-112 — A mention always notifies the mentioned user
109	
110	- **Priority:** must
111	- **Status:** implemented
112	- **Related:** REQ-095, REQ-092, REQ-114
113	- **Implemented by:** `src/server/services/notification-service.ts` — `notify`, `src/server/services/event-registry.ts`
114	- **Verified by:** `tests/services/notification-service.test.ts`
115	
116	The `comment.created` listener reads the mentioned-user-id list straight from the event
117	payload (`REQ-095`) and calls `notify(orgId, 'mention', mentionedIds, payload)` for each,
118	regardless of that recipient's preference for general comment notifications — a mention is
119	its own `NotificationKind`, with its own preference row, distinct from "someone commented on
120	an issue I'm watching."
121	
122	**Acceptance criteria**
123	
124	1. Every user id in a comment's resolved mention list receives a `mention`-kind
125	   notification, subject only to `REQ-114`'s self-notification suppression.
126	2. A recipient who has disabled general comment notifications but not mention notifications
127	   still receives the mention.
128	3. A mention of a user who is not a project member of a private project's issue (`REQ-051`)
129	   still notifies them — mentions bypass the project-membership fan-out narrowing, since
130	   being mentioned is itself evidence of relevance.
131	
132	### REQ-113 — Assignment notifies the new assignee
133	
134	- **Priority:** must
135	- **Status:** implemented
136	- **Related:** REQ-067, REQ-114
137	- **Implemented by:** `src/server/services/notification-service.ts` — `notify`, `src/server/services/event-registry.ts`
138	- **Verified by:** `tests/services/notification-service.test.ts`
139	
140	The `issue.assigned` listener notifies the new assignee (when non-null) with an
141	`assignment`-kind notification; it does not separately notify the previous assignee by
142	default, since being unassigned is a lower-urgency event than being assigned something new,
143	though the previous assignee can still see the change on the issue's own activity feed.
144	
145	**Acceptance criteria**
146	
147	1. Assigning an issue to a user produces an `assignment` notification for that user.
148	2. Unassigning an issue (new assignee `null`) does not by itself produce an `assignment`
149	   notification, since there is no one to notify.
150	3. Reassigning from user A to user B notifies B; whether A is separately notified is
151	   governed by A's own preference for the relevant event class, not by a hardcoded rule.
152	
153	### REQ-114 — Actors are not notified about their own actions
154	
155	- **Priority:** must
156	- **Status:** implemented
157	- **Related:** REQ-111, REQ-112, REQ-113
158	- **Implemented by:** `src/server/services/notification-service.ts` — `notify`
159	- **Verified by:** `tests/services/notification-service.test.ts`
160	
161	`notify()`'s recipient list is filtered to exclude `payload.actorId` before any
162	`Notification` rows are inserted, applied uniformly across every notification kind — mention,
163	assignment, comment activity — so self-assigning an issue or mentioning yourself in a
164	comment (both legal, neither unusual) never produces a notification about your own action.
165	
166	**Acceptance criteria**
167	
168	1. `notify(orgId, kind, recipients, payload)` never inserts a notification whose
169	   `recipientId` equals `payload.actorId`.
170	2. Self-exclusion happens inside the shared `notify()` function, not duplicated per listener,
171	   so a new listener gets it for free.
172	3. A comment mentioning both the author and other members notifies the others but not the
173	   author.
174	
175	### REQ-115 — Notification preferences are per channel and per event class
176	
177	- **Priority:** should
178	- **Status:** implemented
179	- **Related:** REQ-120, DES-130
180	- **Implemented by:** `src/server/repositories/notification-preference-repository.ts` — `getPreference`, `upsertPreference`, `src/server/services/notification-service.ts` — `updatePreference`
181	- **Verified by:** `tests/services/notification-service.test.ts`
182	
183	`NotificationPreference` (`src/types/notification.ts`) is keyed by `(orgId, userId, kind)`
184	and records which `NotificationChannel`s are enabled for that kind — a user might want
185	in-app notifications for everything but digest email only for mentions, not for every
186	comment on every issue they are a project member of.
187	
188	**Acceptance criteria**
189	
190	1. `getPreference(orgId, userId, kind)` returns the effective channel set for that specific
191	   notification kind, not a single global setting.
192	2. A recipient with no explicit preference row for a kind falls back to a documented
193	   default channel set, not an error.
194	3. `updatePreference` writes exactly one preference row per `(orgId, userId, kind)` tuple —
195	   `upsertPreference` overwrites rather than accumulating duplicates.
196	
197	### REQ-116 — Recipients may mark notifications read individually or in bulk
198	
199	- **Priority:** must
200	- **Status:** implemented

---
title: Notifications and digests requirements
id: REQ-NOTIFICATIONS
status: approved
owners: [product-team, t.abara]
last_updated: 2026-05-19
related: [REQ-095, REQ-111, ADR-005, DES-120]
---

## Scope

This document defines the requirements for in-app notifications, per-user preferences, and
the daily digest email: how domain events become notifications, who gets notified and who is
suppressed, read/unread state, and how the digest batches, windows and renders unread items
into one email. It does not define email rendering or delivery mechanics beyond what the
digest needs (`REQ-124`), nor webhook delivery, which has its own retry and backoff story in
`webhooks.md`.

## Context

`src/server/services/notification-service.ts` is the fan-out hub: a single call to
`notify(orgId, kind, recipients, payload)` produces zero or more in-app `Notification` rows,
filtered through each recipient's `NotificationPreference` (`notification-preference-repository.ts`)
and each recipient's applicable feature flags (`resolveChannels` takes a `FlagContext`
because the `digest_email` channel itself is plan-gated, per `REQ-120`). Notification
creation is not the same code path as the domain event that triggers it — `issue-service.ts`,
`comment-service.ts` and the rest never call `notify()` directly; they only `emit()` domain
events, and a set of listeners registered by `registerEventHandlers()` in
`event-registry.ts` are what translate those events into notification calls. This
indirection is what keeps `REQ-114` ("actors are not notified about their own actions")
enforceable in one place rather than duplicated at every emit site.

`Notification` rows are per recipient and per organization (`REQ-110`); there is no
cross-org inbox, which follows the same tenancy discipline as everything else, and a user in
three organizations sees three separate notification counts, one per org, computed by
`countUnread(orgId, recipientId)`.

The daily digest is a distinct concern layered on top: `digest-service.ts#buildDigest`
gathers every unread notification for a recipient inside a bounded window
(`digestWindow()` from `src/lib/date.ts`) and hands the bundle to `renderDigest`, which
produces an email via `renderEmail(template, props)` in `email-service.ts`. The digest job
(`digest-email-job.ts`) runs on the `digest-email` cadence (every 1440 minutes — once a day,
`CADENCE_MINUTES`), calling `shouldRunForOrg(org, now)` to decide whether this tick is the
org's digest hour before doing any real work — most ticks for most orgs are a no-op check,
not a digest send. `sendEmail` never performs network egress in this codebase; it writes the
rendered draft to the log, which is why the corpus can describe email delivery as a real
requirement (`REQ-124`) without needing an SMTP integration to back it.

## Open questions

1. `REQ-012` in `organizations.md` notes that `digestWindow` currently takes a
   `digestHourUtc` integer rather than a full timezone; every requirement in this document
   that references "the org's digest window" inherits that same UTC-hour-not-timezone
   limitation.
2. `REQ-115`'s preferences are per channel and per event class, but there is no requirement
   describing what happens when a recipient's only enabled channel for an event class is
   `digest_email` and the org's plan does not include `digest_email` (`REQ-120`) — whether
   that notification silently has no channel or falls back to in-app is not specified in
   code comments or tests.
3. Whether digest windows should be recomputed if an org changes its digest hour mid-cycle,
   potentially producing a very short or very long first window, is unresolved.

- **Priority:** must
- **Status:** implemented

- **Implemented by:** `src/server/repositories/notification-repository.ts` — `listNotifications`, `countUnread`
- **Verified by:** `tests/services/notification-service.test.ts`

`notifications` carries `org_id` and a `recipient_id`; every read (`listNotifications`,

independent notification state per org — reading everything unread in one org has no effect

**Acceptance criteria**

1. `countUnread(orgId, recipientId)` never includes notifications from a different `orgId`
   even for the same recipient.
2. `listNotifications` requires both an actor (for authorization) and an implicit org scope
   derived from that actor.

3. `sendEmail` accepts an already-rendered `OutgoingEmail` and performs no template logic of
   its own.

200	```mermaid
201	sequenceDiagram
202	    participant Scheduler as jobs/scheduler.tick
203	    participant Job as digest-email-job.runDigestEmailJob
204	    participant DigestSvc as digest-service
205	    participant EmailSvc as email-service
206	    participant NotifRepo as notification-repository
207	
208	    Scheduler->>Job: invoke on digest-email cadence (60 min)
209	    Job->>Job: shouldRunForOrg(org, now) per org
210	    Job->>DigestSvc: listDigestRecipients(orgId)
211	    DigestSvc-->>Job: recipient ids
212	    loop each recipient
213	        Job->>DigestSvc: buildDigest(orgId, recipientId, windowStart, windowEnd)
214	        DigestSvc-->>Job: DigestBundle | null
215	        alt bundle is null
216	            Job->>Job: continue to next recipient
217	        else bundle has entries
218	            Job->>DigestSvc: renderDigest(bundle, recipient)
219	            DigestSvc->>EmailSvc: renderEmail("digest", props)
220	            EmailSvc-->>DigestSvc: RenderedEmail
221	            DigestSvc-->>Job: RenderedEmail
222	            Job->>EmailSvc: sendEmail({to, ...rendered})
223	            EmailSvc-->>Job: void (log write)
224	            Job->>NotifRepo: markRead for each entry
225	        end
226	    end
227	```

229	1. The interval scheduler (ADR-016, cadence table: `digest-email` every 60 minutes) invokes
230	   `runDigestEmailJob(now)` once per tick.

232	   current UTC hour (`shouldRunForOrg`), so a job running every 60 minutes still sends exactly

260	`email-service.ts`'s `renderEmail` and `sendEmail` directly, including the HTML-escaping
261	behaviour documented in DES-134 and the plain-text derivation in DES-133.

`renderDigest` builds a props object for the `"digest"` template consisting of `orgId`,
`recipientName`, `entryCount`, `windowStart`, `windowEnd`, and `headline: bundle.entries[0]
?.title ?? ""` — only the *first* entry's title reaches the rendered email as a standalone
field; the remaining entries are represented only through `entryCount`, a number, not a list.
This means the digest email template itself does not enumerate every notification inside it —
whatever a recipient sees beyond "you have 12 updates, starting with X" is either produced by
the `react-email` template's own rendering of additional props not modeled here, or is simply
not part of the current digest's content, a limitation worth flagging to product since REQ-119
("digest email batches unread notifications into one message") could reasonably be read as
requiring all of them to be visible, not just a count and a headline. `renderDigest` never
calls `sendEmail` itself — it stops at `RenderedEmail`, keeping REQ-124's "rendering is
separated from delivery" true even for the one email template whose content this service, not
a Server Action, decides.

### DES-132 — sendEmail performs no network egress; delivery is a structured log write

- **Satisfies:** REQ-124
- **Decided in:** ADR-016
- **Code:** `src/server/services/email-service.ts` — `sendEmail`

`sendEmail`'s entire body is `logger.info("email.sent", { to: message.to, subject: message
.subject, bytes: message.html.length })` — no HTTP call, no SMTP client, no queue write. The
source comment states the reason directly: "Taskflow has no outbound mail transport by
design — the corpus must build and run offline." This is the accurate contract for anyone
reading `email-service.ts` cold: every call site that awaits `sendEmail` (registration
welcome mail in `auth-service.ts`, password reset in `auth-service.ts`, digest delivery in
`digest-email-job.ts`) is really awaiting a synchronous log write, not a real delivery
attempt, and there is no failure mode to handle beyond whatever the logger itself might throw.
Anyone wiring a real transport in a downstream deployment of this codebase would replace this
function's body without needing to touch any caller, since `OutgoingEmail`'s shape (`to`,
`subject`, `html`, `text`) is already a complete message.

### DES-133 — renderEmail derives plain text from HTML rather than writing both by hand, so the two can never drift

- **Satisfies:** REQ-124
- **Decided in:** ADR-016
- **Code:** `src/server/services/email-service.ts` — `renderEmail`, `toPlainText`,
  `renderBody`, `subjectFor`

`renderEmail` builds HTML first via `renderBody`, a small key/value table renderer that
iterates `Object.entries(props)` (filtering out `null`/`undefined` values) into `<tr>` rows
under an `<h1>` built from `SUBJECTS[template]`, then derives the plain-text version from that
same HTML string via `toPlainText`, a chain of four regex replacements that turns block-level
closing tags into newlines, strips remaining tags, collapses whitespace, and trims. This
one-directional derivation — HTML is the source of truth, text is a projection of it — is
what REQ-124's "rendering is separated from delivery" implicitly protects against a subtler
bug: a hand-maintained plain-text template would eventually drift from the HTML as templates
evolved, silently making the plain-text fallback stale for accessibility or plain-text mail
clients. `subjectFor` appends the organization name to the base subject line
(`${base} — ${orgName}`) whenever `props.orgName` is a string, which is why every rendered
subject in Taskflow's seven templates (`invite`, `digest`, `mention`, `invoice`, `welcome`,
`password-reset`, `overdue`) can carry the org's name without each caller formatting it by
hand — callers that omit `orgName` from their props simply get the bare subject.

### DES-134 — renderBody escapes every value, closing the one XSS surface this renderer has

- **Satisfies:** REQ-124
- **Decided in:** ADR-016
- **Code:** `src/server/services/email-service.ts` — `escapeHtml`, `renderBody`

Every key and value that reaches the rendered HTML table passes through `escapeHtml`, which
escapes `&`, `<`, `>`, and `"` (not `'`, notably — the table cells are not attribute values, so
single-quote escaping was judged unnecessary for this specific rendering context). Since
`renderEmail`'s `props` argument is typed as `Readonly<Record<string, unknown>>` — an open
bag any caller can populate, including from user-supplied data such as an issue title flowing
into a `mention` template — this escaping is the only thing standing between a crafted issue
title and a broken or malicious rendered email, given that the HTML is written to the log and,
in a deployment with a real transport swapped in for DES-132, would be sent as-is to a mail
client that renders HTML. `renderBody` does not attempt to render nested objects or arrays
specially; `String(value)` is called on anything that is not filtered out, so a caller passing
a non-primitive prop gets whatever `String()` produces (`"[object Object]"` for a plain
object), a silent-but-safe degradation rather than a thrown error.

## Sequence: the daily digest job producing one rendered email

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Scheduler as jobs/scheduler.tick
    participant Job as digest-email-job.runDigestEmailJob
    participant DigestSvc as digest-service
    participant EmailSvc as email-service
    participant NotifRepo as notification-repository

    Scheduler->>Job: invoke on digest-email cadence (60 min)
    Job->>Job: shouldRunForOrg(org, now) per org
    Job->>DigestSvc: listDigestRecipients(orgId)
    DigestSvc-->>Job: recipient ids
    loop each recipient
        Job->>DigestSvc: buildDigest(orgId, recipientId, windowStart, windowEnd)
        DigestSvc-->>Job: DigestBundle | null
        alt bundle is null
            Job->>Job: continue to next recipient
        else bundle has entries
            Job->>DigestSvc: renderDigest(bundle, recipient)
            DigestSvc->>EmailSvc: renderEmail("digest", props)
            EmailSvc-->>DigestSvc: RenderedEmail
            DigestSvc-->>Job: RenderedEmail
            Job->>EmailSvc: sendEmail({to, ...rendered})
            EmailSvc-->>Job: void (log write)
            Job->>NotifRepo: markRead for each entry
        end
    end
```

1. The interval scheduler (ADR-016, cadence table: `digest-email` every 60 minutes) invokes
   `runDigestEmailJob(now)` once per tick.
2. The job filters organizations to those whose configured `digestHourUtc` matches the
   current UTC hour (`shouldRunForOrg`), so a job running every 60 minutes still sends exactly
   one digest per organization per day.
3. For each eligible org, `listDigestRecipients` returns everyone who has opted at least one
   notification kind into digest-only delivery.
4. `buildDigest` is called per recipient with a one-day window ending at `now`; a `null`
   result — plan-gated or genuinely empty — is skipped without further work.
5. A non-null bundle is rendered through `renderDigest`, which itself delegates to
   `email-service.ts`'s `renderEmail`.
6. `sendEmail` "delivers" the message by writing a structured log line; there is no network
   call to fail.
7. The job marks every digested notification's `notificationId` as read via
   `notificationRepo.markRead`, which is what keeps the next tick inside the same UTC hour
   from re-sending the same entries — the job, not `digest-service.ts`, owns this idempotence.

## Failure modes

| thrown error | resulting error code | caller behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| none from `buildDigest`/`listDigestRecipients`/`renderDigest` under normal operation | n/a | the job's own `try`/`catch` around each recipient increments `result.failed` and logs, per `digest-email-job.ts`'s structure; a single recipient's failure does not stop the loop |

| none from `sendEmail`/`renderEmail` under normal operation | n/a | `renderEmail` cannot fail on well-typed props; a non-serializable prop degrades to `String()` output rather than throwing (DES-134) |

## Test coverage

`tests/jobs/digest-email-job.test.ts` exercises `shouldRunForOrg`'s hour matching and the
job's end-to-end loop, which is the only test coverage that reaches `buildDigest`,

`email-service.ts`'s `renderEmail` and `sendEmail` directly, including the HTML-escaping
behaviour documented in DES-134 and the plain-text derivation in DES-133.

40	own event bus design deliberately avoids by having no timers in it at all.
41	Tomas wanted one clock, one place that decided what was due, and one drain
42	loop, not seven uncoordinated ones.

45	
46	`src/server/jobs/scheduler.ts` is a single interval, started from
47	`src/instrumentation.ts` at process boot via `startScheduler()`, ticking
48	every `TICK_INTERVAL_MS` (60,000 ms — once a minute). `CADENCE_MINUTES` is a
49	`Readonly<Record<JobKind, number>>` declaring, per job kind, the minimum gap
50	between two runs: `digest-email` 60, `overdue-issues` 60, `webhook-delivery`
51	1, `usage-rollup` 15, `search-reindex` 1,440 (once a day), `cleanup-archived`
52	1,440, `trial-expiry` 360 (every six hours). This single table is the
53	authoritative cadence policy the ADR-005 sketch never actually specified —
54	this ADR is where "how often does each kind of scheduled work run" got a
55	real, reviewable answer, expressed as one number per job kind rather than
56	scattered per-feature timer logic.
57	
58	`tick(now: Date)` — deliberately taking an explicit `Date` parameter rather
59	than reading the clock itself — is the actual unit of work: for each
60	`JobKind`, `isDue(kind, now)` checks whether `now` is at least
61	`CADENCE_MINUTES[kind]` minutes past `lastRunAt.get(kind)` (or has never
62	run at all, which is always due); if due, it records `lastRunAt` and
63	`enqueue()`s a job row via `src/server/jobs/queue.ts`, then the tick calls
64	`drain()` once to process whatever is now pending. Splitting `tick()` out
65	from the `setInterval` callback specifically enables the test suite to drive
66	scheduling deterministically with an explicit clock — the module's own
67	comment states this directly — instead of a test having to wait a real
68	minute for the interval to fire, which is why `startScheduler()`'s callback
69	is a thin wrapper calling `tick(new Date())` and nothing else. The timer
70	itself is `.unref()`ed, so — matching the philosophy behind the event bus's
71	handler isolation — a pending scheduler tick never blocks process shutdown;
72	the module's comment states plainly that "a scheduler that blocks shutdown
73	is worse than one that misses the last tick." `stopScheduler()` clears the
74	interval and the `lastRunAt` map together, so a restarted scheduler starts
75	clean rather than remembering stale cadence state from a previous run.
76	`isSchedulerRunning()` is a simple boolean check used by health diagnostics
77	and tests.
78	
79	Each job kind's actual work — `runWebhookDeliveryJob`, the overdue-issue
80	sweep, digest rendering, and so on — lives in its own module under
81	src/server/jobs/, invoked by the queue's `drain()`, not by the scheduler
82	directly; the scheduler's only responsibility is deciding *when* a kind of
83	work becomes due and handing it to the queue.

86	
87	**What this buys the team.** One clock, one cadence table, one drain loop —
88	adding an eighth job kind (which happened once already, `trial-expiry`, added
89	in April 2026 for REQ-142) is a one-line addition to `CADENCE_MINUTES` plus a
90	new job module, not a new timer to wire up and separately guard against
91	outliving the process. Because `tick()` takes an explicit clock, the test
92	suite exercises real cadence behavior — "does `overdue-issues` actually wait
93	sixty minutes between runs" — with fast, deterministic tests advancing a fake
94	clock, rather than either skipping that coverage or accepting slow
95	real-time tests. The `.unref()`ed timer has, in practice, meant a graceful
96	shutdown never hangs waiting on a scheduler tick, something Jan Novak's SRE
97	team specifically checked for during the first production-shaped deployment
98	rehearsal and found already handled, rather than a gap they had to raise.

102	one-minute cadence is about as tight as this scheduler can express without

9	
10	**Date:** 2026-03-04
11	**Attendees:** t.abara (chair), j.novak, m.lindqvist, d.okafor
12	
13	## Agenda
14	
15	1. Post-incident review of the digest storm from two days ago
16	   (`postmortem-2026-03-02-digest-storm.md`).
17	2. Decide whether `ADR-005`'s original cadence framing needs revision.
18	3. Draft the cadence policy that will become `ADR-016`.
19	
20	## Discussion
21	
22	Tomas opened by walking the group through the incident timeline once more, focusing on
23	the two-factor root cause: the scheduler's in-memory `lastRunAt` resetting on restart,
24	and `markRead` failures not undoing an already-sent digest. He posed the central
25	question directly: does fixing this mean making scheduler state durable, or does it mean
26	something else?
27	
28	Jan argued strongly against durable scheduler state as the fix, walking through the
29	counterfactual: even with a persisted `lastRunAt`, the storm's actual repeat-send
30	mechanism — unread notifications re-qualifying for inclusion on every subsequent

id: OPS-NOTES-2026-03-04

**Date:** 2026-03-04
**Attendees:** t.abara (chair), j.novak, m.lindqvist, d.okafor

## Agenda

1. Post-incident review of the digest storm from two days ago
   (`postmortem-2026-03-02-digest-storm.md`).
2. Decide whether `ADR-005`'s original cadence framing needs revision.
3. Draft the cadence policy that will become `ADR-016`.

## Discussion

Tomas opened by walking the group through the incident timeline once more, focusing on
the two-factor root cause: the scheduler's in-memory `lastRunAt` resetting on restart,
and `markRead` failures not undoing an already-sent digest. He posed the central
question directly: does fixing this mean making scheduler state durable, or does it mean
something else?

Jan argued strongly against durable scheduler state as the fix, walking through the
counterfactual: even with a persisted `lastRunAt`, the storm's actual repeat-send
mechanism — unread notifications re-qualifying for inclusion on every subsequent
eligible window because `markRead` never completed — would have fired regardless of
whether the restart happened. He was blunt that "we got unlucky with timing on a
restart, but the bug was already there and would have surfaced eventually from ordinary
lock contention alone." Deji agreed and raised a related point: even setting aside this
specific bug, treating the scheduler's cadence table as a *correctness* guarantee rather
than a *dispatch throttle* was itself a category error baked into how `ADR-005`
described the job system originally. `ADR-005` said jobs would run "hourly by default,"
which reads as a promise about frequency, but says nothing about what a job is
responsible for guaranteeing about its own idempotence between runs.

Mira pushed the group to be precise about what the new policy should actually say, since
"be more idempotent" is not an actionable engineering statement on its own. The group
worked through a concrete rule: every job kind's cadence entry in `CADENCE_MINUTES`
governs when the job is *eligible* to be dispatched, and is explicitly not a guarantee
against the job running more than once within that window — restarts, manual triggers
(see `runbook-scheduler-and-queue.md`'s procedures), and legitimate overlapping windows
can all cause more-frequent-than-cadence execution, and every job body must be written
assuming that can happen. For `digest-email` specifically, the group agreed the
send-then-markRead sequence needed to move from "best effort, log and move on" to
"retry the markRead on the very next eligible tick if it failed," narrowing but not
eliminating the duplicate-send window.

This is the meeting where the group explicitly revised the framing `ADR-005` had set:
`ADR-005`'s cadence language is being narrowed by what becomes `ADR-016`, and everyone
in the room agreed this should be recorded plainly in `ADR-016`'s Context section as a
correction, not just a new idea layered on top without acknowledging the earlier
document said something looser. Tomas volunteered to draft `ADR-016` with this framing
and circulate it the next day.

## Decisions

1. Scheduler cadence (`CADENCE_MINUTES`) is reframed as a *dispatch throttle*, not a
   correctness guarantee — this narrows the framing `ADR-005` originally used and will
   be recorded as such in `ADR-016`.
2. Durable scheduler state (persisting `lastRunAt`) is explicitly rejected as the fix for
   this incident class; job bodies must be idempotent under more-frequent-than-cadence
   execution instead.
3. `digest-email-job`'s `markRead` failure path will retry on the next eligible tick
   rather than only logging and waiting for the notification to fall out of its natural
   window.
4. `ADR-016` will be drafted to formally supersede this portion of `ADR-005`'s framing.

One more thread came up near the end that Tomas wanted on the record even though it did
not change the outcome: should the digest job move to a per-recipient lock, so two
overlapping runs literally cannot process the same recipient concurrently, rather than
relying on `markRead` idempotence alone? Deji was skeptical — introducing locking into a
job system that has deliberately stayed lock-free (`queue.ts` has no concept of a
mutex, only sequential draining within one process) would be a meaningfully bigger
change than the retry-on-next-tick fix the group already agreed on, and he was not
convinced the digest storm's actual failure mode required it: the overlapping runs in
this incident were sequential ticks, not truly concurrent execution within the same
process, since `drain()` processes jobs one at a time in a single event loop. Jan
confirmed this matches his understanding of the queue's execution model — there is no
parallelism to race against within one process, only the *appearance* of overlap across
separate ticks. The group closed this thread by agreeing locking is unnecessary given
that understanding, and that the retry-on-next-tick fix directly addresses the actual
mechanism at fault.

## Follow-ups

- Tomas to draft `ADR-016` and circulate for review before end of week.
- Jan to add the queue-depth and duplicate-send alerting items from the postmortem's
  action list in parallel with the ADR draft, since they do not depend on the ADR being
  finalized first.
- Mira to review every other job kind's body against the "must tolerate
  more-frequent-than-cadence execution" rule once `ADR-016` lands, not just
  `digest-email`.

## How a daily digest actually gets sent for one workspace

**The governing requirement** is `docs/requirements/notifications-and-digests.md` (id `REQ-NOTIFICATIONS`), specifically REQ-119 ("Digest email batches unread notifications into one message"), tightened by REQ-120 (plan-gating), REQ-121 (window bounded by last send), REQ-122 (empty digest not sent), and REQ-123 (emits `digest.due` before rendering). These are implemented by `src/server/services/digest-service.ts` (`buildDigest`, `renderDigest`, `listDigestRecipients`) and `src/server/jobs/digest-email-job.ts` (`runDigestEmailJob`, `shouldRunForOrg`).

**Design/architecture it rests on:**
- `docs/design/service-digest-and-email.md` (`DES-DIGEST-EMAIL`) splits "what to send" (`digest-service.ts`) from "how to send it" (`email-service.ts`, which only writes a structured log — `sendEmail` performs no network egress, per DES-132).
- `docs/adr/ADR-016-interval-scheduler.md` is the architectural decision that governs *when* anything runs at all: one process-wide interval scheduler (`src/server/jobs/scheduler.ts`), ticking every `TICK_INTERVAL_MS` (60,000 ms, once a minute), with a single `CADENCE_MINUTES` table giving each job kind a minimum gap between dispatches. ADR-016 explicitly narrows ADR-005's looser "hourly by default" framing into a precise "dispatch throttle, not a correctness guarantee" — a distinction hashed out in `docs/ops/notes-2026-03-04-digest-cadence-review.md` after the incident in `docs/ops/postmortem-2026-03-02-digest-storm.md`.

**What decides the job is due (job-kind level, not per-org):** `scheduler.ts`'s `isDue(kind, now)` compares `now` against `lastRunAt.get(kind)` using `CADENCE_MINUTES["digest-email"]`, which in code is **60** (`src/server/jobs/scheduler.ts:14`). So the scheduler makes the `digest-email` job *eligible to be dispatched* once per hour, not once per day — every eligible tick, `runDigestEmailJob(now)` runs and walks *every* organization.

**What decides it's due for *this* workspace:** inside that hourly run, `digest-email-job.ts`'s `shouldRunForOrg(org, now)` (lines 84‑87) checks `org.archivedAt === null && now.getUTCHours() === org.settings.digestHourUtc`. Only orgs whose configured digest hour matches the current UTC hour proceed past that `continue` in `runDigestEmailJob`'s loop (line 36), followed by the plan check `isEnabled("digest_email", buildFlagContext(null, org))` (REQ-120). For a matching org, `listDigestRecipients(orgId)` and `buildDigest` (windowStart = now − 24h) produce the actual email via `renderDigest`/`sendEmail`, and each digested notification is marked read via `notificationRepo.markRead` — the mechanism that keeps the *next* hourly tick, still inside the same UTC hour in edge cases, from re-sending.

**What verifies it:** `tests/jobs/digest-email-job.test.ts` — e.g. "uses the org's configured digest hour to pick the window", "skips an org whose digest hour has not arrived", "skips an org whose plan does not include digest_email", "does not resend a digest for an already-covered window" — which `docs/test/traceability-req-to-test.md` maps directly to REQ-119–REQ-124.

## The eligibility-vs-frequency distinction, and the doc's number

These are two different cadences, and the requirements doc conflates them:

- **Job eligibility** (how often the `digest-email` job kind is dispatched, org-agnostic): governed by `CADENCE_MINUTES["digest-email"]` in `scheduler.ts`, which is **60** — hourly. This is confirmed both by ADR-016's cadence table ("`digest-email` 60") and by `service-digest-and-email.md`'s sequence diagram ("invoke on digest-email cadence (60 min)").
- **Per-workspace delivery frequency** (how often any one org actually receives a digest): **once a day**, produced entirely by `shouldRunForOrg`'s UTC-hour match against `org.settings.digestHourUtc` — the scheduler cadence has nothing to do with this outcome beyond being frequent enough (hourly) to catch each org's one matching hour.

`docs/requirements/notifications-and-digests.md` (line 42) states: "The digest job (`digest-email-job.ts`) runs on the `digest-email` cadence (every 1440 minutes — once a day, `CADENCE_MINUTES`)". That sentence describes the *per-workspace* outcome correctly (once a day) but misattributes it to `CADENCE_MINUTES`, and gets the actual code value wrong — `CADENCE_MINUTES["digest-email"]` is 60 in `src/server/jobs/scheduler.ts`, not 1440. 1440 minutes is the org-batch job cadence for daily jobs like `search-reindex`/`cleanup-archived` per ADR-016, not digest-email's dispatch cadence. So the "1440" in the requirements doc is simply wrong as a description of `CADENCE_MINUTES`; the number that document should have used for the scheduler's dispatch throttle is 60, with the once-a-day figure being a downstream *effect* of `shouldRunForOrg`, not a property of the scheduler cadence table at all.
